sources.title: American Statistical Association releases statement on statistical significance and P-values: provides principles to improve the conduct and interpretation of quantitative science
sources.version: ASA news release, 7 March 2016, announcing the ASA Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values and reproducing its six principles. Companion article DOI 10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108
sources.locator: Page 2, the numbered list of six principles: principle 1 (a p-value can indicate incompatibility between data and a specified statistical model), principle 2 (it measures neither the probability that the studied hypothesis is true nor the probability that data arose by chance alone), principle 3 (conclusions should not rest only on passing a threshold), principle 5 (a p-value or statistical significance does not measure effect size or importance). Page 1, the remark on an arbitrary threshold.
sources.license: Copyright American Statistical Association; the release is distributed publicly by the association with no open-content reuse licence displayed, and no reuse licence is relied on here

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify that a statistical body has stated as formal principles that a p-value can indicate incompatibility between data and a specified model, that it measures neither the probability that the studied hypothesis is true nor the probability that data arose by chance alone, that it does not measure the size or importance of an effect, and that conclusions should not rest solely on a threshold. No principle is quoted or reproduced; each is restated in this lesson's own words and applied to invented teaching data. No wording, list ordering, example, or figure from the release is reused.

agentAccess.notes: Route selection was governed by an agent-access check made before substantive reading. The publisher route for the journal article, https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108, was checked first and excluded: that host's robots file carries an explicit record disallowing all paths to the named AI crawler GPTBot, which this project treats as a restriction on agent ingestion, so the article was neither opened nor processed there. The association's own distribution of the statement was used instead. The amstat.org host publishes no robots file (the route returns HTTP 404), declares no machine-readable crawler or text-mining directive, and exposes no terms page restricting automated reading; the release is the association's own public announcement of its own statement. The three-page PDF was retrieved over plain HTTPS in a single request with no login, paywall, rate-limit breach, or access-control bypass. Readers should note that this record covers the ASA news release, which reproduces the six principles in full, and not the peer-reviewed article, which remains behind a route this project does not use.

sources.title: Statistical tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power: a guide to misinterpretations
sources.locator: Statistical testing section: definitions of a test statistic, of the null hypothesis, and of the P value as the probability that the statistic is at least as large as observed if every model assumption held; the point that the P value tests the whole model; the separation of alpha from the P value. Moving from tests to estimates: effect sizes with P above 0.05 form the 95 per cent interval. Common misinterpretations of single P values: the listed items and refutations used in scene 4.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to verify the definitions of a test statistic, a null hypothesis, and a P value; the point that the probability is computed under every model assumption rather than under the tested hypothesis alone; the distinction between a cut-off fixed in advance and a P value computed from data; the correspondence between a 95 per cent interval and the set of hypothesised values not rejected at the 0.05 level; and the four corrections this lesson teaches about what a P value does not report. No wording, numbered item, table, figure, worked example, or organisational scheme from the guide is reproduced, adapted, or closely paraphrased; every case, number, and study in this lesson is invented and the instructional sequence is original.

agentAccess.notes: The NCBI robots file was retrieved and read before substantive access. Its wildcard user-agent record disallows the generic PMC article route /pmc/articles/, so that route was not used. The full text was read through the public NCBI BioC REST endpoint at /research/bionlp/RESTful/pmcoa.cgi/BioC_xml/PMC4877414/unicode, which no record in the file disallows, and the stable PubMed record was used for bibliographic metadata. The article is open access under CC BY 4.0. One HTTPS request was made, with no login, paywall, rate-limit breach, or access-control bypass.

sources.title: Statistical hypotheses, verification of
sources.publisher: European Mathematical Society and Springer (Encyclopedia of Mathematics)
sources.version: Encyclopedia of Mathematics wiki article, revision oldid 49601, adapted from an original article by M. S. Nikulin in the Encyclopaedia of Mathematics, ISBN 1402006098
sources.locator: Opening definition of a statistical hypothesis as a non-empty subset of the set of admissible probability distributions for the observed random vector, and the identification of two competing hypotheses in which one is called the null hypothesis and the other the alternative hypothesis; the accompanying distinction between simple and compound hypotheses
sources.license: CC BY-SA 3.0 and GNU Free Documentation License, as stated on the encyclopedia's copyrights page

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to confirm the standard framing of a null hypothesis and an alternative hypothesis as two competing statements about the distribution behind the observations, with the null being the one held fixed for testing. No wording, notation, worked example, or organisation from the entry is reused, the entry's measure-theoretic presentation is deliberately not reproduced, and the displayed share-alike licence is therefore not relied on.

sources.title: Significance level
sources.publisher: European Mathematical Society and Springer (Encyclopedia of Mathematics)
sources.version: Encyclopedia of Mathematics wiki article, revision oldid 34286, adapted from an original article by L. N. Bol'shev in the Encyclopaedia of Mathematics, ISBN 1402006098
sources.locator: Opening definition of the significance level of a statistical test as the probability of incorrectly rejecting the basic hypothesis being tested when that hypothesis is valid, together with the description of a test being constructed through a selected function of the observations that takes small values when the hypothesis holds and large values when it fails
sources.license: CC BY-SA 3.0 and GNU Free Documentation License, as stated on the encyclopedia's copyrights page

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only to confirm that the significance level is a probability attached to a test in advance and that a test is built from a function of the observations chosen to grow as the data depart from the hypothesis. The entry's further development of this quantity as an error rate belongs to a later lesson and is deliberately not taught here. No wording, notation, or example from the entry is reused, and the displayed share-alike licence is not relied on.
